Kansas Formally Applauding the Lynchers.
Recently we published an account of the lynching of a negro in Kansas for the atrocious and unpardonable crime of rape. We now have the satisfaction to note that a mass meeting of the citizens of a neighboring town adopted the following resolutions, formally thanking the lynchers for their speedy administration of justice to the criminal:

Be it Resolved, That we citizens of Baxter Springs, in meeting assembled, approve of the hanging of Lawrence, and that we heartily and sincerely thank A. B. C. D. and others of said company who so bravely and at their own peril accomplished that which we all desired should be done.

Resolved Further, that we hereby extend to the good people of our neighboring town of Girard this expression of regret that time and circumstances brought the termination of a detestable criminal's life within the limits of their town; that we hope their community may never be agitated and outraged by the commission of any similar or other crime, and that for any damage or damages done to property in said town of Girard by the said "company of men" that claims for the same be reported to the "citizens committee" of Baxter Springs for adjustment:

madison-madison.A3:
GEORGIA AND FLORIDA.
THE NEWS OF THE TWO STATES
TOLD IN PARAGRAPHS.
W. H. Culver, of Sparta, died a day or two ago.
John Brown, of Joselyn, was robbed of $10, Saturday night.
Warrentown boasts a citizen aged 82 who still goes fox hunting.
Madison prohibitionists will wait a year before calling another election.
Benjamin Hill, colored, sacrificed three fingers in a Macon saw mill Thursday.
Luke Rice, a prominent contractor of Augusta, died at Hartford, Conn., a day or two ago.
Four white persons were taken from Macon to the State Lunatic Asylum at Milledgeville, Thursday.
Five damage suits are docketed for the next term of Sumter Superior Court, all for the sum of $10,000 each.
Gens, J. B. Gordan and A. R. Lawton telegraphed their regrets at being unable to attend the Griffin re-unions.
Recorder Foster, of Augusta, will not resign, but will fight it out on his line with the City Council if it takes all summer.
Two waiters at a Macon hotel fought a duel with plates, Thursday. Considerable crockery was smashed but no arrests were made.
Bartow Lyle was almost decapitated while working in a mine near Villa Rica, Thursday, by a cave in of rock and gravel. He will die.
Henry Simpkins, a negro physician, of Macon, has been married to his third wife, the first two being still living and not divorced.
Anderson Dugger's patent clover huller, a machine costing $500, was burned near Adairsville Thursday, presumably from a hot journal, together with $90 worth of clover.
At Harmony Grove Jimmie Johnson, while on his way to school, stuck a thorn in his hand, causing a very serious injury. It is thought his arm will have to be amputated.
A post office has recently been established with the name of Inglewood at the home of Judge James Bishop, about fourteen miles from Eastman, on the Ocmulgee river.
The people of Sunny Side have about decided to change the name of the place to Kell, in honor of Capt. J. M. Kell, something of whose history is known to every school boy in every nation.

The election to fill the vacancy in the Town Council of Harlem, advertised to take place on Monday, went by default in consequence of the absence of the Mayor and other members of the board.

In Poik county a negro, 96 years old, has recently cut a full set of teeth, upper and lower, and is in good health for one of his advanced years. This makes the third set of natural teeth that he has had.

Harmony Grove Signal: Any one wanting their fingers sawed off can get their wants supplied by tackling Tom Sumpter's shingle mill. There has only been two sawed off in the last fifteen days.

W. M. Timmons, of Jesup, was aroused a night or two ago by a noise at his hen house. He proceeded to the place, when he suddenly came in contact with a large catamount. The two soon separated, and have not been so intimate since.

The postal authorities will give Bottsford better mail service on and after September first, a semi-weekly mail, going out from Americus on Wednesday and Saturday, then going into effect. An effort is being made to get a tri-weekly mail for Lamar.

Aaron McLeod, colored, attempted to outrage Mrs. J. W. Mullis, a white lady, near Eastman a day or two ago, but her cries brought assistance before she suffered bodily harm. A posse of men were in pursuit of the negro at last accounts, and lynching was considered possible.

Col. Towers, principal keeper of the penitentiary, has issued an order for Bill McGaughey to be taken from the chain-gang and carried to Walton county for the murder of his wife. She died since he was incarcerated from injuries that he gave her. He was sent up for a different offense.

The town council of Elberton has passed a registration ordinance for the town requiring twelve months residence in the State, six months in the county, thirty days in the town, and the payment of all taxes before a citizen can register and vote. The town elections come off the last of September, but there will be no exciting question before the people, as prohibition is an established fact in the town after the expiration of the present license.

The docket now filling up with cases for trial at the October term of Fulton Superior Court does not indicate any abatement in the number of divorce cases. At the last term of the court there were 35 divorce cases set for trial, and the number promises to be fully as large at the approaching term. About three-fourths of the cases are from negroes. One negro woman gave as a reason for asking a divorce that she had been living with her husband for five years and was tired of him.

Ogden Olmstead, of Taylor's creek, Liberty county, has gone to New York, where he goes to visit relatives. There is a rumor also that Mr. Olmstead goes to claim a legacy which was left him by his grandmother. Report says that just at the breaking out of the war, when all communication was cut off, a snug little sum of money was deposited in bank to the credit of Ogden Olmstead, who was then but a small lad. Ogden was in ignorance of the fact until a short time ago.

Coleman Chancey, colored, formerly engaged in the manufacture of naval stores in the vicinity of Eastman, but who has been operating works in Wilcox county for the past year or two, has skipped the country. Before leaving he provided himself with $1,500 in ready cash, by disposing of his interest in his works in Wilcox county to A.T. Wiggs, of Dubois. It appaers also that Coleman had tired of his family as well as his location, since Lucretia Johnson, a former colored school matr in Eastman, accompanied him in his flight.

Elberton Gazette: The colored band of Elberton was employed by the prohibitionists of Madison county last week to furnish music there on the day of the election. On the day before the election the band went over, but on their arrival they were informed that they would possibly be sater by returning to this side of the river, which they did without ceremony. A Postmaster Caught Robbing the Malla. KNOXVILLE, TENN., Aug. 22.—This morning United States Marshal Ivins brought in Col. A. S. Mariner, postmaster at Careyville, who was caught robbing the mails. The case was worked up by Post Office Inspector Charles E. Dosser. He procured warrants for the arrest of Mariner, and yesterday, in company with the Marshal and United States District Attorney J. C. J. Williams, confronted him in the Post Office at Careyville, and showed the Postmaster that he had certain evidence of his rifling registered letter packager. Mariner was placed under guard at the hotel. While there he was observed to drop something from his window. Marshal Ivins picked up the paper, and found it to be a letter from Dr. J. Overton, addressed to Senator Isham J. Harris, mailed at Careyville on Tuesday. Mariner failed to give a $2,000 bond, and is now in Knoxville jail. Col. Mariner was formerly commandant of cadets at the University of Tennessee, and several years ago was Republican candidate for Mayor of Knoxville. Grand Army Day at Chautauqua.
CHAUTAUQUA. Aug. 22.—A Grand Army service was held in the Amphitheatre this afternoon. Five hundred veterans of the war, led by a band, marched into the hall. The Chautauqua choir sang a number of war songs, including Julia Ward Howe's "Battle Hymn of the Republic" and "Marching through Georgia." Gen. Clinton B. Fisk was introduced as orator of the day. He said that 2,850,000 men enlisted in the Union army between Sumter and Appomattox. Three hundred thousand of them sleep in seventy-nine national cemeteries, and 134,000 sleep in nameless graves. He said Grant was the country's greatest son, the chiefest captain of our time. Grant, he said, believed in the Bible, and attributed his success in life to his godly mother, who taught him to reverence religion and to worship the Supreme Being. After the singing of the Gloria Patria by the choir and the immense audience, Bishop Foss of Minnesota pronounced the benediction.

A Body Washed Up at Esopus.

KINGSTON, Aug. 22.—Last Wednesday the body of an unknown man was washed on the Esopus shore, near Pell's Dock. It was apparently that of a person about 40 years of age. He was five feet eight inches in height, weighed 150 pounds, had dark hair, reddish moustache, and wore side whiskers. The general appearance was that of an American of intelligence and refinement. Some papers were found in his pockets, which afford some clue to his identity, and may be the means of unraveling some mysterious disappearance. The man was attired in a new suit of dark gray cloth, wore new laced shoes, a white shirt with turned-down collar, and black necktie. Coroner Contant of Esopus has charge of the remains. He empanelled a jury, which adjourned until Thursday evening next to await developments.

Incinerated in a Steel Furnace.

HARRISBURG, Aug. 22.—Paul Susteeskle, a Pole, was employed as a top filler at one of the stacks in the Pennsylvania Steel Works near this town. This evening, as they were preparing to close the works, he was adjusting the bell top. As the bell was lowered the gas gathered in the stack, and Susteeskle stooped to adjust the covering. He inhaled the gas, became asphixiated, and tumbled headlong into the fiery furnace. Death was instantaneous. His associates attempted to rescue his remains by the use of grappling hooks from the top. A double handful of bones, clothing, and flesh was all that could be recovered.

Kn-Klux Outrages in Tennessee.

NASHVILLE, Aug. 22.—Masked men took Samuel Low, colored, of Duck River Bottom, Humphreys county, from his cabin, and gave him over 100 lashes. Twenty lashes were given West Regan, colored, at the same time, and he was ordered to leave the county, which he did immediately. John Gorin, a colored school teacher, was warned to depart or suffer the consequences. He departed. A negro who recently attempted to escape a beating was shot and killed. No arrests have been made.

samuel-low-1885-08-21.A4:
Whipping Negroes.
NASHVILLE, Tenn., Aug. 23.—For months past a more or less bitter feeling has existed between certain white and black citizens of Humphreys county. Recently a negro who attempted to escape from a crowd which intended to administer a beating to him was shot and the next morning his dead body was found near his cabin. All efforts to discover the perpetrators of the crime were futile. Other negroes were taken out and brutally lashed and yet no arrests were made. Information was received to-day that a mob of seven disguised men visited the home of Samuel Low, (colored), in the Duck river bottom and, presenting revolvers at the frightened man, dragged him from his bed. They conveyed him to the woods and administered more than one hundred blows with iron-wood switches, larcerating his back in a horrible manner. West Regan (colored), who had been secured by the mob before they found Low, was also beaten, being given twenty blows and ordered to leave the county, which he did at once. Low is seriously ill and will be unable to leave his bed for some days. John Gorin, a colored school teacher in this vicinity, found on his door a note warning him to leave the county or suffer the consequences. Gorin, who was very much alarmed, departed immediately. The best citizens of Humphreys county strongly condemn these outrages and will likely call on the governor to offer a reward for the apprehension of the guilty parties.

CHICAGO.
Rev. Moody Condemned—Masonic—Political—Personal—Social—Dramatical, Etc.

The colored people of this city are loud in their condemnation of Rev. Moody. He has, by his preaching, established the color line, and aroused and encouraged dissension wherever he has gone. His doctrine and preaching are insults to the intelligent American people, and they should not tolerate it.—John Maxwell is the only colored undertaker in the city.—The Masonic Grand Lodge of this State will meet October 13.—An important meeting of the Grand Consistory of the 32d degree Masons, was held Sunday afternoon. The Illustrious John W. Dunmore was present, ably assisted by Robt. C. Waring. The occasion was the admission of James Reed to the 32d degree.—Geo. Brown, the champion prize fighter of the city, is now in the insane asylum at Jefferson.—The Cook County Convention of colored men will meet September 28, to elect thirty delegates to the State Convention at Springfield, October 15.—Mrs. A. F. Bradley has returned, after a pleasant visit in Ohio.—Mrs. S. Taylor, of Butterfield street, was called to Springfield by the death of a relative.—Wm. L. Darrow has returned from the East.—H. D. King is still confined to his room with a severe spell of sickness.—Martin Gibson has openly boasted that he will kill any lawyer that prosecutes him in a law suit now pending between him and his wife. Mrs. Gibson has secured the services of Attorney John G. Jones to prosecute her case, and it will be done to the bitter end.—The Corinthian Commandery No. 18, K. T., has postponed the picnic until September 8. It will be held at the same place.—The drama "Out in the Streets," under the management of Mrs. Ida M. Dempcy, was presented at Immanuel Congregational Church on Friday evening, August 21, and was a dramatic as well as financial success. The Rev. G. C. Booth reports the sum of $85 on hand, with some returns not yet received. The following was the cast:

Colonel Wayne—an inimitable old gentleman.....Mr. Frank B. Waring
Mrs. Wayne.....Miss Hattie Warner
Solomon Davis—a heartless landlord.....
Mr. D. P. French
Matt Davis, his son—a "hard case".....
Mr. J. D. Alexander
The Widow Bradford—turned "out in the streets" by Davis....Miss Ida M. Dempcy
Minnie Bradford, her daughter, aged eight years....Little Alice Thomas
North Carolina Pete—Mr. Wayne's Negro servant....Mr. Justin Du Bois
Nina Wayne—daughter of the Colonel.....
Miss Allie Booth
Dr. Medfield—in love with Nina.....
Mr. G. M. Crisup

The characters were well sustained throughout, but especial mention must be made of Mr. Waring, whose impersonation was excellent, and of Mr. Du-

bois, who assumed his part at twenty-four hours' notice, the gentleman to whom the part was originally assigned being called away suddenly.—The entertainment given by the Golden Fleece Lodge, at the Casino roller skating rink, was largely attended. The programme included bicycle riding, speeches by Leroy Hayes, J. C. Buckner and others, and a five mile race on rollers for the Illinois championship, which prize included a gold medal and $5.00 in money, was won by Master Samuel Houston.—The picnic given by Bethesda Baptist and Immanuel Congregational churches, announced for to-day, was postponed on account of rain.

"I hope that no soldier who goes into the abolition war will ever return to Iowa alive."—Copperhead whiting, Democratic Candidate for Governor, during the war.

The Albia Democrat is very inoffensive in its partisanship just now. It is laying low for a duck of a post-office.

We cannot help it, but Sherman, of the Newton Democrat, cannot and will not get that postoffice. He is not able to knock down that persimmon. It is beautiful only for Flowers.

Charges have been filed against some Alaskan officials on the score of drunkenness. If that commits, some of the Iowa Democratic officials can be taken in. Specifications can easily be obtained.

—One of the things that President Smith should have on exhibition at the State Fair should be a specimen of the "offensive partisan." How would Agnew do, removed at Osceola to make way for a tramp?

The Kellogg Enterprise, Greenback, tremblingly squeaks out of the high grass: "The Greenback party is as much in control of bosses as either of the old parties. The bosses should be relegated to the rear, or the party will die." And die it will!

Among the Democrats the matter most in demand is Mr. Gillette's letter accepting the Democratic platform in its entirety, or a declination. Mr. Gillette will have to "take suthin,'" with or without sugar, as he pleases, but he will have to tip the schooner—and that right quick.

The re-nomination of Senator Hutchinson by the Wapello Republicans presages victory. He is backed by Hon. F. M. Epperson and Mr. La Force for the House. The Republicans of that county know how to make a hard fight and will do it. They will win, and win handsomely.

The Chicago News, independent for money at all times, says: "In his speech at Mount Gilead, Ohio, Senator Sherman was justified in saying that no act in President Cleveland's administration had done more to lower it in the opinion of conservative men than the pardon of Lieut. Mullen, of the Cincinnati police."

You do not hear any Democratic paper suggesting the name of any Democratic soldier for appointment to such a place as the Pension Agency. Why don't some editor forget copperhead Whiting long enough to suggest that brave soldier, Col. Mackey, for the place? We can endorse his bravery, for we saw it tested grandly and to his lasting honor.

The Poweshiek Republicans have nominated a splendid ticket, and will elect it from top to bottom. It is headed by W. H. Redman for the House, one of the hard fighting, hard hitting boys, who will run like a prairie fire. The other nominees: Treasurer, W. J. Johnson; Auditor, Joseph Satchell; Sheriff, A. M. Hogan; Superintendent, S. W. Heath; Surveyor, Arthur L. Kemper; Coroner, H. Whitcomb.

Dr. Beardsley, the new Chairman of the Republican State Central Committee, was formerly editor of THE HERALD—and is the second editor of this paper so honored—the late Henry C. Leighton, having served in that responsible capacity. Dr. Beardsley will make a splendid chairman, and one who will cause a brilliant campaign. George Roberts as secretary will be found a most efficient man there as he has been so found in all other places.

In 1884 the straight Republican vote in Iowa was 197,089, and the fusion vote, taking in Democrats and Greenbackers or Democrats and Butler men, was 177,316. This gave the Republicans a plurality of 18,311, in a total vote of 375,877. Still, some very foolish fellows think that under the cry of free whisky they can carry Iowa in this year of grace. They cannot do it, and they know it. What a cursing of fusion there will be by Democrats in November, when the certainty of defeat will be a fact backed by Republican majorities!

With the tail of the ticket, Moore, rampant to kick the Bible out of the public schools, and to prevent the children from singing "In the Sweet Byeand-Bye," and the copperhead at the head in favor of taxing all churches and institutions of that character, what a bouquet of loveliness is presented to the decent voters of Iowa by the Democracy and their handful of greenbackers. The "Sweet Bye-and-Bye" will have nothing sweet for that outfit after November shall have come with its 200,000 protecting ballots.
